Great app ideas often start on paper. Turn them into interactive tools with Gemini. Here’s how.



Upload a photo of your sketch, like an app mock-up, habit tracker, or game board to Gemini.
Select the Canvas tool and ask Gemini: "Can you code this app?" Gemini reads your visual and writes the code.
Test your tool in the preview window. Gemini can adjust colors, fonts, or features in real time.



Next time inspiration strikes, bring it to life with Gemini.

Raising awareness about lung cancer on YouTube

Susan Wojcicki, former CEO of YouTube, passed away from lung cancer in 2024. She was diagnosed as a healthy mom of five with no known risk factors. Anyone with lungs can get lung cancer, and no one deserves it.



Now the Susan Wojcicki Foundation, led by her family and leaders across science, tech and philanthropy, is launching a YouTube channel to change the conversation around lung cancer. The channel brings creators together with leading experts, scientists, and the lung cancer community to help raise awareness and make the science clear, approachable, and part of everyday conversation.

When’s the last time you checked who (or what) has access to your Gmail inbox? Run a quick Google Security Checkup and protect your email with three quick and easy steps:



Review signed-in devices.


Remove old third-party app access.


Confirm recovery information.

How to use Gemini to update your resume

In four simple steps:



1. Open Gemini and ramble at it about all your past roles.

2. Add this prompt: “Act as a professional resume writer. Use my raw, unedited notes about my past work and turn it into four high-impact resume bullets for a _______ role. Start each bullet with a strong action verb. Keep the tone executive, clear, and ATS-friendly.”

3. Chat back and forth to adjust details, tone, and focus.

4. Copy and paste it into your resume when it’s done.

Testing robotic systems for deep space missions

Google Cloud and NASA are collaborating to test proof-of-concept robotic assistants for future missions to the Moon and Mars.


These robotic assistants are powered by models fine-tuned on Google Cloud edge computing and trained in Google DeepMind’s MuJoCo physics engine, and are built to assist astronauts with daily logistics and critical tasks, like retrieving and preparing medical tools during an emergency.

Data-backed secrets to holiday shopping

Shop smarter this holiday season with our When to Buy Guide, based on historical data showing when holiday discounts may hit their peak. Mark your calendars:



👃 Shop early for fragrances for the best deals and inventory.

🎮 Promotions for video games and consoles peak during Black Friday weekend.

🧳 For travel gear, shop Black Friday for accessories and late December for suitcases.

🤖 If electronic toys are on your kids’ wish lists, you’ll find the steepest markdowns in the final shopping stretch.

💻 Once you create a skill, just type the @ symbol and the skill’s name directly in the prompt bar.

Helping bring the world’s first large-scale, near-zero emissions steel plant online

Sep 17, 2026

1 min read

Google is partnering with Stegra to help bring their large-scale, green hydrogen-based, near-zero emissions steel plant online.

Ben Townsend

Head of Infrastructure & Sustainability

Jenna Stauffer

Head of Strategic Priorities, Climate Operations

Share
00:00
Listen to article
1:59 minutes

We’re partnering with Stegra to help bring the world’s first large-scale, green hydrogen-based, near-zero emissions steel plant online. The steel is designed to meet the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) definition for near-zero emissions steel production, marking an important step toward addressing the impact of the hard-to-decarbonize steel industry.

While traditional steel manufacturing relies on coal to process iron, Stegra’s plant in Boden, Sweden, will use renewable electricity to generate green hydrogen. The hydrogen is then reacted with iron ore to produce iron. Stegra estimates that removing coal from the process can cut emissions by up to 95% compared to traditional blast furnace manufacturing.

Under the new agreement, Google will receive environmental attribute certificates (EACs) from a portion (up to 91,000 metric tons) of the steel produced in Stegra’s first year of production. Companies purchase EACs to drive demand for sustainably produced materials, address construction emissions, and help scale and finance these early stage technologies.

By supporting innovative technologies and partnering with coalitions like the Sustainable Steel Buyers Platform, we hope to bring more green building materials to market and increasingly incorporate them into our own operations. We estimate this can reduce the embodied carbon emissions from data center infrastructure by up to 40%. News from Google is Google's official publication for the latest company announcements, updates, and behind-the-scenes storytelling. Our contributors include hundreds of the world’s leading engineers, product managers, and internet pioneers who work directly on products and services like Google Search, Ads, Gemini, Maps, Android, Chrome, Pixel, and Play.

News from Google also regularly features opinions and perspectives from Google’s senior leadership, including CEO Sundar Pichai, Google DeepMind co-founder and Chair Demis Hassabis, and President of Global Affairs Kent Walker.

News from Google has published thousands of articles covering topics ranging from our work in generative AI with Google DeepMind to the latest Google Cloud innovations. News from Google is also the central hub for breaking news and announcements from annual events like Google I/O and Made by Google.

News from Google is designed to grow and change as Google does, so as we introduce new products and technologies they will have a home on this blog. And alongside the biggest news of the day, we’ll also share quick product tips and ideas to make your life easier.

In short: If there’s anything you want to know about what’s happening at Google right now, News from Google is where you should start.

Noteworthy authors

Googlers from across the company contribute to News from Google — ranging from engineers and designers to doctors and scientists. Here are a few examples:

Sundar Pichai

Sundar is the CEO of Alphabet and Google and serves on Alphabet’s Board of Directors. Under his leadership, Google has been focused on developing products and services, powered by the latest advances in AI, that offer help in moments big and small.

Demis Hassabis

Demis Hassabis is the co-founder and Chair of Google DeepMind, one of the world’s leading AI research groups. DeepMind has produced landmark research breakthroughs such as AlphaGo, the first program to beat the world champion at the game of Go, and AlphaFold, which was heralded as a solution to the 50-year grand challenge of protein folding.

James Manyika

James is a senior vice president at Google. He focuses on technology and society, including areas ranging from AI to the future of work and the digital economy, computing infrastructure, sustainability, and other areas that have the potential for broad impact on society. Prior to Google, he spent over 25 years at McKinsey & Company, including serving on its board, and is now senior partner emeritus and chair emeritus of the McKinsey Global Institute (MGI).

Ruth Porat

As President and Chief Investment Officer, Ruth is responsible for the company’s corporate investments and investment vehicles, including GV and CapG, the Other Bets investment portfolio, Real Estate and Workplace Services, and other company infrastructure. She was previously SVP and CFO of Alphabet and Google.

Kent Walker

Kent is the President of Global Affairs at Google and Alphabet, where he works at the intersection of technology, policy, and legal issues. He joined Google in 2006, and currently oversees the company’s engagement with governments around the world, content policies, and philanthropic efforts.

Rick Osterloh

Rick Osterloh leads Platforms & Devices, a group of products and services that bring the best of Google’s innovation in AI, software, and hardware to users, partners, and developers. This includes the overall Android platform, Google Play, Chrome browser, ChromeOS, Google One, Google Photos, the Pixel portfolio, Nest, Fitbit, and more. He works closely with partners across the ecosystem, and oversees multiple Google products that serve more than a billion users each.

How to follow us

You can also find the latest news and stories from Google on our official social channels — including Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn, X, and TikTok — and our weekly email newsletter.

Helping bring the world’s first large-scale, near-zero emissions steel plant online

Sep 17, 2026

1 min read

Google is partnering with Stegra to help bring their large-scale, green hydrogen-based, near-zero emissions steel plant online.

Ben Townsend

Head of Infrastructure & Sustainability

Jenna Stauffer

Head of Strategic Priorities, Climate Operations

Share
00:00
Listen to article
1:59 minutes
Read AI-generated summary

We’re partnering with Stegra to help bring the world’s first large-scale, green hydrogen-based, near-zero emissions steel plant online. The steel is designed to meet the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) definition for near-zero emissions steel production, marking an important step toward addressing the impact of the hard-to-decarbonize steel industry.

While traditional steel manufacturing relies on coal to process iron, Stegra’s plant in Boden, Sweden, will use renewable electricity to generate green hydrogen. The hydrogen is then reacted with iron ore to produce iron. Stegra estimates that removing coal from the process can cut emissions by up to 95% compared to traditional blast furnace manufacturing.

Under the new agreement, Google will receive environmental attribute certificates (EACs) from a portion (up to 91,000 metric tons) of the steel produced in Stegra’s first year of production. Companies purchase EACs to drive demand for sustainably produced materials, address construction emissions, and help scale and finance these early stage technologies.

By supporting innovative technologies and partnering with coalitions like the Sustainable Steel Buyers Platform, we hope to bring more green building materials to market and increasingly incorporate them into our own operations. We estimate this can reduce the embodied carbon emissions from data center infrastructure by up to 40%. In 2025, we successfully integrated low-carbon concrete, steel, or a combination of both in over 20 construction projects.
